title: Fetching Data on the Server
summary: Fetch where the data is used, run requests in parallel, stream slow parts with Suspense, and read cookies, headers, and search params.
intro: Almost every page in a shop shows data from somewhere else: products, reviews, a cart. Where and how you fetch it decides how fast the page appears, and the difference between a page that shows up in a quarter of a second and one that keeps a visitor staring at a blank screen for two. This lesson fetches Trailhead's data in Server Components, runs requests side by side, streams the slow parts so the rest shows at once, avoids asking twice for the same thing, reads cookies and the URL's search string, and says when fetching in the browser is still the right call.

steps.title: Fetching in Server Components
steps.body:
In the React course, data came in an effect or through TanStack Query, after the page had already loaded in the browser. That meant loading flags, a request that only left once JavaScript ran, and an empty page for search engines. In a Server Component, you fetch before the page is sent, so the first HTML already has the data in it.

## Await in the component

A Server Component can be `async`, so getting data is a plain `await`: call `fetch`, query a database, or call a function that does either. No `useEffect`, no `useState` for the result, no loading flag. The component waits, and then returns JSX with the data in it. React and Next.js handle what to show while it waits, which the part on streaming covers.

The `fetch` here is the same one you know from the browser, built into Node.js. Next.js adds a little to it on the server, like logging each call during development, but a plain `fetch` with a full URL works as you'd expect. Since it runs on the server, it isn't subject to CORS, the browser's cross-origin rules from the web course, and it can send secret headers.

## Keep the fetching in one module

Rather than calling `fetch` in every page, Trailhead keeps all of it in `lib/`, as the lesson on Server Components set up. `lib/api.ts` holds `apiFetch`, which adds the base URL from `API_URL` and turns any status outside 200 to 299 into an `ApiError` with the status on it. Now it also returns `unknown` instead of pretending to know the shape, and takes a `session: true` option that forwards the visitor's login cookie, which the part on request data uses. `lib/products.ts` builds `listProducts`, `getProduct`, and `getReviews` on top of it. Pages import those and never see a URL.

## Check the shape with zod

The API is another program, and it can change or break. Recall zod from the React course: a schema describes the shape you expect, and `parse` either returns data of that type or throws. Parsing at the edge of your app means a surprise from the API fails loudly in one place, with a clear message, instead of quietly showing `undefined` somewhere on a page. It also gives you the TypeScript type for free with `z.infer`.

## Errors and missing data are different things

Two things can go wrong, and they deserve different treatment:

- **Missing data is a normal answer.** A product slug that doesn't exist gets a 404 from the API. That's not a crash, so `getProduct` returns `null`, and the page calls `notFound()`, as the routing lesson showed.
- **A real failure is an error.** The API is down, or answers 500, or sends a shape zod rejects. Let it throw. The nearest `error.tsx` catches it and shows its message, the rest of the page keeps working, and the server's log gets the full details with a digest to match.

Don't catch every error and return empty data. A shop that shows No products when the API is down looks like a shop with nothing to sell, and nobody gets told that something broke.

examples.title: The product functions
examples.prompt: `lib/products.ts`, with the schemas and the three functions pages use. `apiFetch` and `ApiError` come from `lib/api.ts`.
examples.explanation: Each function asks the API for one thing and parses the answer. The list comes in a page envelope, `{ items, page, pageSize, total }`, so `listProducts` parses that and returns just the items. zod objects ignore keys they don't list, so the API can add fields without breaking anything. `getProduct` turns a 404 into `null`, and `getReviews` turns one into an empty list, since a missing product has no reviews. Any other error, like a 500 or a shape that doesn't match, is thrown. `encodeURIComponent` keeps a category with odd characters from breaking the URL. Every component that uses `Product` or `Review` now gets its type from the schema, so the type and the check can't drift apart.

examples.title: When the API is down
examples.prompt: Stop the Trailhead API, run the production build with `npm run start`, and open `/products`. The page shows the products section's error box. This is the server's terminal.
examples.explanation: The first lines are the server starting. The `⨯` line is the failure: `fetch failed`, with a stack that points into the built server code, then the **cause**, the real reason, which is `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:4000`, nothing listening on the API's port. That's the connection refused from the web course's lesson on reaching a server, seen from the server's side. The `digest` is the same code the error box shows in the browser, where the message itself is hidden. Start the API again, press Try again in the error box, and the products load: `retry` renders the failed part once more.

steps.title: Sequential and parallel requests
steps.body:
A page that needs several pieces of data can wait for them one at a time, or all at once. One at a time is what you get by default when you write one `await` after another, and it's the most common reason a Next.js page is slower than it should be.

## The waterfall

Each `await` pauses the function until its promise settles. So this:

```tsx sketch
const product = await getProduct(slug);
const reviews = await getReviews(slug);
```

asks for the reviews only after the product has arrived, even though the reviews don't depend on the product at all. The requests run like steps on a staircase, which is why it's called a **waterfall**. Two requests of 200 and 900 milliseconds take 1,100 together, and every extra step adds its full time.

```diagram server-data-fetching-waterfall
One after another, the times add up. Side by side, the page waits only as long as the slowest request.
```

## Promise.all

When two requests don't depend on each other, start them both before waiting on either. `Promise.all` takes a list of promises and gives back one promise for all their results, in the same order:

```tsx sketch
const [product, reviews] = await Promise.all([getProduct(slug), getReviews(slug)]);
```

Both requests leave at once, and the page waits only for the slower one: 900 milliseconds instead of 1,100. If either one fails, `Promise.all` fails at once with that error, which here is what you want, since the error boundary should show. When you'd rather keep going with whatever succeeded, `Promise.allSettled` waits for all of them and tells you which ones failed.

## Start early, await late

You don't always want to wait for everything in one place. The pattern that scales is to **start** a request as early as you can, as a promise, and **await** it only where the value is needed. A call without `await` starts the request and gives you the promise straight away:

```tsx sketch
const reviews = getReviews(slug); // the request leaves now
const product = await getProduct(slug); // wait only for this
```

The reviews are on their way while the page waits for the product, and some component further down can await them, or a client component can read them with `use`, as the previous lesson showed.

## Siblings fetch in parallel on their own

Next.js renders sibling components side by side. If a layout renders two Server Components next to each other, and each fetches its own data, both requests start at once without any `Promise.all`. The same goes for a layout and its page: Next.js starts rendering both together. So a good habit is to let each component fetch what it shows. Waterfalls come back when one component awaits something and only then renders the child that does the next fetch. When you see that shape, start the child's request earlier, in the parent, and pass the promise down.

## Measure it

In development, the terminal shows each page request with the fetches it made, and how long each took. The examples below are the same page written both ways, with that log. To make the log name each fetch's full address, add `logging: { fetches: { fullUrl: true } }` to `next.config.ts`. The timings in this lesson came from the Trailhead API started with `TRAILHEAD_DELAYS=1 node trailhead-api/server.mjs`, so each answer takes about as long as a real API's would.

The product took 203 milliseconds and the reviews 904. Added together, that's the page's whole wait, because the reviews request didn't leave until the product had arrived. `cache skip` means the response wasn't kept for later, the default when nothing asks for caching, which the next lesson changes.

steps.title: Streaming with Suspense
steps.body:
Running requests side by side made the page wait 900 milliseconds instead of 1,100, but a visitor still sees nothing for most of a second, all because of the reviews, which sit at the bottom of the page. Streaming lets the server send the parts that are ready and fill in the slow parts as they arrive, in the same response.

## Suspense boundaries

Recall `Suspense` from the React course: you wrap a part of the tree in `<Suspense fallback={...}>`, and while anything inside is still waiting, React shows the fallback in its place. On the server, a Suspense boundary is also a seam in the response. Next.js sends the page up to each boundary right away, with the fallbacks in place, and keeps the connection open. When a component inside a boundary finishes, the server sends its HTML down the same response, with a tiny script that swaps it in for the fallback. No extra request, and no JavaScript of yours.

```diagram server-data-fetching-stream
The shell arrives first, then the product, then the reviews, each replacing a placeholder, all in one response.
```

In step 1, at about 25 milliseconds, the browser has the header and menus, with Loading product… where the page goes. That's the `loading.tsx` from the routing lesson, which is itself a Suspense boundary around the page. In step 2, the product arrives and replaces it, with a skeleton where the reviews will go, because the reviews sit in their own boundary. In step 3, the reviews arrive and replace the skeleton. The HTTP response is one long one, sent in chunks. HTTP/1.1 calls that **chunked** transfer, and you saw its header, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, in the lesson that created the project.

## loading.tsx or an inline boundary

A `loading.tsx` wraps a whole page, so nothing of the page shows until its slowest part that isn't in a boundary of its own is done. An inline `Suspense` wraps one part, so everything outside it can show first. Use both: `loading.tsx` for the moment between a click and the page's first data, and inline boundaries around the parts that are slower than the rest, like reviews, recommendations, or anything from a slow service.

Put each boundary around the smallest piece that waits, and keep data the piece needs inside it. The component that awaits must be **inside** the boundary. If the page itself awaits the reviews and then renders `<Suspense>`, the boundary has nothing left to wait for, and the page is back to waiting for everything.

## Skeletons that hold their space

A fallback that's shorter than what replaces it makes the page jump when the content arrives, pushing what's below it down just as someone is about to click. That jump is **layout shift**, which the web course measured as CLS, one of the Web Vitals. A good fallback is a **skeleton**: gray shapes the same size as the real content, so the swap changes what's in the boxes, not where they are. Give the skeleton the same heights and gaps as the finished list.

## What streaming doesn't fix

Streaming changes when parts of the page arrive, not how long the data takes. The reviews still take 900 milliseconds. What changes is that the visitor reads the product and can add it to the cart in the meantime. And a page that streams has already sent its `200` status before the slow parts finish, which is why the routing lesson's late `notFound()` couldn't change the status. Decide anything that changes the status, like whether the product exists, before the first boundary when you can.

examples.title: A product page that streams its reviews
examples.prompt: `app/products/[slug]/page.tsx`. The reviews request starts first, the page waits only for the product, and the reviews stream in their own boundary.
examples.explanation: `getReviews(slug)` without `await` starts the request first, so it runs while the page waits for the product. `Reviews` is a small async Server Component that awaits the promise, and it sits inside the boundary, so only it waits. `ReturnType<typeof getReviews>` is the promise's type, taken from the function. The skeleton has two rows, each `h-12` tall like a real review, with the same gaps, so the swap doesn't move anything. `aria-label` gives screen readers something to say about the empty shapes. The page next to this file still has its `loading.tsx` for the moment before the product arrives.

examples.title: Watching the chunks arrive
examples.prompt: A small Node.js script, `stream-times.mjs`, that prints when each chunk of a response arrives, how big it is, and which of four phrases it contains. Run it with the production server running.
examples.explanation: Run it with `node stream-times.mjs http://127.0.0.1:3005/products/ember-stove`. Node.js gives the response body as a stream, so the `for await` loop gets each chunk as it lands. The first four, at about 25 milliseconds, are the shell: the page's `head`, the header, and Loading product…. At 228 the product arrives, with the reviews skeleton, whose `aria-label` holds the words Loading reviews. At 927 the reviews arrive, the newest first, Boils fast. The last few chunks carry the RSC payload for hydration, which mentions the loading text again. Without the reviews' boundary, nothing after the shell would arrive until 927.

examples.prompt: `getProduct` in `lib/products.ts` wrapped in React's `cache`, as in the snippet above, with nothing else changed. The dev log for one visit.

steps.title: Request data: cookies, headers, and searchParams

examples.title: An account page that reads the session
examples.prompt: `app/account/page.tsx`. `getCurrentUser`, in `lib/session.ts`, calls `apiFetch("/me", { session: true })`, returns `null` for a 401, and parses the user with zod.
examples.explanation: The page itself reads nothing from the request, so its heading and the Checking who you are… fallback are prerendered during the build. `Greeting` reads the session through `getCurrentUser`, so it waits for the request, inside the boundary. With no `th_session` cookie, the API answers 401, `getCurrentUser` returns `null`, and the page links to the login page. The text is one template string, so the HTML holds it as one piece, which the next example's `grep` relies on. In the build's route table, `/account` is `◐`, a partial prerender, for exactly this split.

examples.title: The account page with and without a session
examples.prompt: With the production server running, ask for `/account` without a cookie, then log in as Sam at the Trailhead API, keep the cookie it sets in `cookie`, and ask again with it.
examples.code:
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3005/account | grep -o 'Signed in as [^<\\]*\|Log in to see your orders' | head -1
cookie=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -D - http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/auth/login -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"email":"sam@example.com","password":"trailhead"}' | grep -o 'th_session=[^;]*')
curl -s -H "Cookie: $cookie" http://127.0.0.1:3005/account | grep -o 'Signed in as [^<\\]*\|Log in to see your orders' | head -1
examples.explanation: The first request has no cookie, so the streamed part says to log in. The second line posts Sam's email and password to the API's login, and `grep` keeps the `th_session=...` part of the `Set-Cookie` header it answers with, a new random value on every login. The third sends it in a `Cookie` header, the way a browser would after logging in. `apiFetch` forwarded it to the API's `/me` endpoint, which knew whose session it was. The `grep` keeps the first match, since the text appears twice in the response: once in the HTML and once in the RSC payload. Both answers came from the same build: the shell was identical, and only the part inside the boundary changed.
examples.output:
Log in to see your orders
Signed in as Sam (sam@example.com)

examples.title: Filtering by a search parameter
examples.prompt: `app/products/page.tsx` reads `category` from `searchParams` inside its boundary and passes it to `listProducts`. Ask for the tents and list the product links.
examples.explanation: Three tents came back, rendered on the server for this URL. The page's `ProductGrid` component awaits `searchParams`, checks that `category` is a string and not an array, and calls `listProducts("tents")`, which adds `?category=tents` to the API call. The category links in the products layout point at these URLs, so clicking one renders the grid again on the server with the new value, while the layout and its links stay as they are. The heading and the Loading products… fallback stay in the prerendered shell, since only the grid reads the URL.
examples.output: Ridge 2P Tent Alpine 1P Tent Basecamp 4P Tent

steps.title: Fetching in the browser when you must
steps.body:
Server Components fetch most data best, but not all of it. Some data changes while the visitor is looking at it, and some only matters after they do something. For those, fetching in the browser is still the right tool, and knowing when keeps you from forcing everything through the server.

## When the browser should fetch

- **Data that changes while the page is open.** Stock that's selling out, a live score, a chat. A Server Component renders once per request, so its data is a snapshot. Something has to ask again.
- **Data that follows an interaction.** Search suggestions as someone types, the next page of an infinite list, a preview when someone hovers. These depend on what the visitor does after the page loads.
- **Per-user data on a page that's otherwise the same for everyone,** when you'd rather keep the page fully static and fill in the personal part in the browser. Streaming it from the server, as the account page did, is usually simpler, but this is an option.

## Refreshing from the server

The simplest way to get fresh data is often to ask the server to render again. `router.refresh()`, from the router you met in the routing lesson, fetches the current page's RSC payload again, and React swaps in what changed. Client state, like a quantity someone picked, survives, because the client components stay mounted. Call it on a timer, or after an event, and the Server Components re-run with fresh data, with no API calls in the browser at all.

## TanStack Query in the browser

When a client component needs to fetch on its own, use TanStack Query, as in the React course: keys, caching, retries, and refetching all work the same. Two differences apply in Next.js. Its `QueryClientProvider` lives in a client wrapper, as the previous lesson showed. And the browser can't call an API that needs a secret key, or one that doesn't allow your site's origin, so such calls go through your own server, in a Route Handler, which a later lesson covers.

## A server promise, read with use

The middle path from the previous lesson: a Server Component starts the request and passes the promise to a client component, which reads it with `use`. The data comes from the server, with its secrets and closeness to the API, and the client component can then add state, like sorting or a filter, on top.

## Choosing

| The data | Fetch it |
| --- | --- |
| The same for everyone, changes rarely | In a Server Component, and cache it (next lesson) |
| Depends on the cookie or URL | In a Server Component, inside `Suspense` |
| Changes while the page is open | Server Component plus `router.refresh()`, or TanStack Query |
| Follows typing, scrolling, or hovering | In a client component, with TanStack Query |
| Needs a secret key | Only on the server: a Server Component or a Route Handler |

Start from the top of the table, and move down only when the data needs it.

examples.title: A component that refreshes the page
examples.prompt: `components/refresh-every.tsx` renders nothing and asks the server for a fresh page on a timer. A stock line could use `<RefreshEvery seconds={30} />`.
examples.explanation: This is an effect in its proper role, from the React course: syncing with something outside React, here a timer. The cleanup clears the interval when the component unmounts or `seconds` changes. Each `router.refresh()` re-renders the current page's Server Components on the server and sends the new payload. The stock number updates, while client state, like the quantity in the picker, stays as it was. It costs one server render per visitor per interval, so pick an interval to match how fast the data really changes, and prefer streaming events from the server, as the Route Handlers lesson shows, when seconds matter. Every fetch in this lesson asked the API again on every visit. The next lesson keeps the results and shares them between visitors, so most pages are ready before anyone asks.

recap:
- Server Components await data before the HTML is sent, with no effects, loading flags, or CORS.
- Keep fetching in a server-only module, and check every response's shape with zod.
- Return null or an empty list for missing data, and let real failures throw to error.tsx.
- One await after another is a waterfall. Start independent requests together with Promise.all, or start them early and await late.
- Suspense boundaries stream: the shell comes first, and each slow part replaces its fallback in the same response.
- fetch is memoized within one render, and React's cache does the same for any function.
- cookies(), headers(), and searchParams are async and make their part dynamic, so read them inside Suspense.
- Fetch in the browser only for live or interaction-driven data, with router.refresh() or TanStack Query.
